unit.title: Perform advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A drawing asks for a plate shape cut to ±1.5 mm. What should you do before cutting?
options: Cut it slightly oversize by eye and grind it to fit later
Mark it accurately, allow for the cut width, and set up a guide
Cut it freehand as fast as possible to reduce distortion
Ask another trainee to cut it, then check it afterwards

questions.stem: Which process is best for cutting a shape in 6 mm stainless steel?
options: Oxy-acetylene cutting
Oxy-fuel cutting, large nozzle
Air carbon arc gouging
Plasma arc cutting

questions.stem: What eye protection is suitable for air carbon arc gouging?
options: A welding helmet with about a shade 12 filter
Gas welding goggles with a shade 5 filter fitted
Clear safety glasses on their own
Dark sunglasses under a cap

questions.stem: Why is hearing protection needed for air carbon arc gouging?
options: The welding machine's cooling fan runs much louder than usual
The air hose may burst at any time
The arc and air blast are very loud and can damage hearing
The carbon electrodes crack loudly when they cool

questions.stem: When gouging, where should the stream of molten metal be pointed?
options: Towards the wall so that it is caught and stops
Down at your feet so you can see where it lands
Away from people, hoses, cylinders and anything that can burn
Straight up into the air so that it cools before landing

questions.stem: Why must the ventilation be good when cutting or gouging painted or coated steel?
options: So that the plate cools down quickly before it can distort
Large amounts of harmful fume and smoke are given off
So the air jet has enough clean air to work
So the sparks are blown out of the workshop

questions.stem: Why does thicker plate need a bigger cutting nozzle?
options: More cutting oxygen is needed to burn through the full depth
A bigger nozzle makes the cut much narrower on thick plate
A bigger nozzle uses less gas than a small one
A bigger nozzle can be held much further away from the plate

questions.stem: What is a radius bar (circle-cutting guide) used for?
options: Measuring the thickness of plate before cutting
Holding the nozzle while the torch is cooling
Cutting straight lines along a clamped guide
Guiding the torch round a fixed centre to cut circles

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of using a guide or cutting trolley for long straight and bevel cuts?
options: It lets you cut without any need to wear goggles
It means no marking out is needed
It allows any nozzle size at all to be used for the job
It keeps the nozzle height, angle and line steady

questions.stem: To cut a 30° bevel on a plate edge for a single-V butt weld, how far is the nozzle tilted from the vertical?
Two plates each have a 30° bevel. What is the included angle of the joint?
How is a root face (land) made on a flame-cut bevel?
options: By cutting a second bevel from the underside
By heating the sharp edge until it melts and goes round
By leaving or grinding a small square edge at the bottom
By hammering the sharp edge flat on an anvil

questions.stem: When piercing a hole in plate with oxy-fuel, what should you do as the cutting oxygen is turned on?
options: Raise the nozzle a little and tilt it so the slag blows away
Push the nozzle down so it touches the plate
Turn the oxygen on fully at once with the nozzle on the plate
Hold the nozzle very still and as close as possible

questions.stem: When cutting a hole out of the middle of a plate, where should you pierce to start?
options: Right on the marked line of the hole
In the good metal just outside the line
In the waste metal inside the hole, away from the line
At the edge of the plate, then cutting right in to the hole

questions.stem: Why are small tabs (bridges) sometimes left uncut until last when cutting long narrow strips?
options: To mark where the next strip will start
To make the hot strips easier to lift out by hand
To save cutting oxygen on long jobs
To hold the strip in place and reduce distortion

questions.stem: When cutting round a template with a hand torch, what is most important?
options: Pressing the nozzle hard against the template edge
Keeping the template firm and the nozzle a set distance off it
Using a carburising flame so that the template itself does not burn
Cutting as fast as possible so the template stays cool

questions.stem: How should a cut be started on thick plate, such as 50 mm?
options: In the middle of the plate, with the nozzle flat to the surface
At the edge, with the top corner preheated to bright red first
Anywhere, with full oxygen on before the steel is hot
At the edge, moving fast before the steel gets hot

questions.stem: On a thick plate cut, the bottom of the cut lags behind the top. What is this lag called?
options: Drag
Bevel
Dross
Notch

questions.stem: When oxy-fuel cutting thin steel sheet, what helps to stop it melting and buckling?
options: A large nozzle and a slow travel speed
A carburising flame with the torch held still
A small nozzle, tilted forward in the direction of travel
The gouging nozzle held flat to the sheet

questions.stem: When cutting a pipe by hand, how should the nozzle be held?
options: Always vertical, whatever part of the pipe you cut
Laid flat along the pipe surface, as for gouging a groove
At 45° to the pipe surface all the way round
Square to the pipe surface, pointing at the pipe's centre

questions.stem: Why should you check where the cut-off piece will drop before finishing a cut?
options: So it cannot fall onto feet, hoses or people
So that it lands flat and does not get scratched
So that it falls into the slag tray for weighing
So that it cools slowly and does not harden

questions.stem: What is oxy-fuel gouging used for?
options: Joining two plates together without filler metal
Hardening the surface of a steel plate by heating it red
Cutting holes through thick plate quickly
Removing metal to form a groove, such as a faulty weld

questions.stem: How does a gouging nozzle differ from a normal cutting nozzle?
options: It has no preheat holes at all, only oxygen
It is curved and gives a softer, low-speed oxygen stream
It is straight, with a much smaller hole in the centre for oxygen
It burns only fuel gas, with no oxygen used

questions.stem: In oxy-fuel gouging, what mainly controls the depth of the groove?
options: The length and colour of the gas hoses
The size of the gas cylinders in use
The nozzle angle and the travel speed
The colour of the outer flame

questions.stem: How does air carbon arc gouging remove metal?
options: A jet of oxygen burns the metal away
A spinning disc grinds the metal out
An arc melts it and an air jet blows it away
A jet of nitrogen gas cuts it like plasma

questions.stem: Which current is normally used for air carbon arc gouging of steel with standard electrodes?
options: DC, electrode positive (DCEP)
DC, electrode negative (DCEN)
High-frequency AC only
Any current, it makes no difference

questions.stem: Where should the air jets be when the carbon electrode is set in the gouging torch?
options: Above the electrode, on the side away from the work
To one side, pointing back at the operator
Behind the torch handle, away from the arc
Under the electrode, between it and the work

questions.stem: Why is the carbon electrode moved forward in the torch as it burns away?
options: So that the electrode can cool down fully in the air jet
To keep the stick-out short, with the air near the arc
To make the arc longer and the groove wider
So that fewer electrodes are used on each job

questions.stem: With the same electrode angle, what happens to the groove if you travel faster?
options: The groove gets deeper
The groove gets shallower
The groove gets much wider
The air pressure goes up

questions.stem: Why is a gouged groove usually ground before it is welded?
options: To make the groove deeper than the drawing shows
To polish it so that it looks good when it is inspected
To cool it down quickly before welding begins
To remove the carbon-rich skin, which can cause cracks

questions.stem: What mainly sets the width of an air carbon arc gouge?
options: The electrode diameter
The air pressure setting
The length of the cables
The shade of the filter

questions.stem: What is plasma gouging?
options: Cutting straight through the plate with a plasma torch held at 90°
Joining two plates with a plasma arc and filler wire
Removing metal in a groove, with a gouging tip at a low angle
Cleaning rust off plate with the plasma air jet

questions.stem: Why should a plasma torch be held at the right stand-off distance, or used with a drag shield?
options: To protect the nozzle and keep the cut square and clean
To make the arc longer so it reaches thicker plate
To let the operator work without any eye protection
To stop the compressed air from being used up

questions.stem: A plasma cut face has a bevel and a lot of dross. Which is a likely cause?
options: The plate was cleaned before cutting
The air filter had just been drained
The nozzle or electrode is worn
The work clamp was on bright metal

questions.stem: Why may high-carbon steel need preheating before flame cutting?
options: So that the cut is faster and uses less gas
So that the plate will not need marking out
So that the slag sticks to the bottom of the cut
To stop the cut edge becoming hard and cracking

questions.stem: How is the angle of a cut bevel checked?
options: With a set of feeler gauges and a rule
With a bevel protractor or weld gauge
With a tape measure only
By eye, against the drawing

questions.stem: A cut part must be 300 ± 1.5 mm. Which measured size must be rejected?
What is a notch (gouge mark) on a cut face, and why is it a problem?
options: A deep step left in the face; it can start cracks
A smooth, even face that needs no further work
A thin layer of oxide that protects the edge from rust
A fine drag line that shows the speed was right

questions.stem: After flame cutting a shape, how are sharp corners and small notches finished?
options: Filled with weld metal and then left just as they are
Hammered flat with a heavy hammer
Ground smooth to the line, without going undersize
Painted over so they cannot be seen

questions.stem: What is washing, in thermal cutting?
options: Cleaning the plate with water before the cut is started
Burning off bolt or rivet heads flush with the surface
Cooling the cut edge with water to harden it
Rinsing the slag off the cutting table at the end of the day

questions.stem: Why is the root of a butt weld that is welded from both sides back-gouged before the second side is welded?
options: To remove the unsound root so the weld fuses to sound metal
To make the plate thinner so it is easier to weld
To cool the first side down before the second side is welded on
To check the plate thickness with a gauge

questions.stem: Before gouging out a crack in a weld, what should be done first?
options: Gouge only the middle part of the crack, to save time and gas
Weld over the crack first to seal it in
Paint over it so it is easier to see
Find both ends of the crack so that all of it is removed

questions.stem: When you finish air carbon arc gouging, what should you do with the electrode stubs and equipment?
options: Throw the hot stubs into the general waste bin
Leave the machine on and the air running to cool it
Put hot stubs in a metal container, switch off, close the air
Leave the stubs on the floor until they are cool

questions.stem: The cutting oxygen lever on a torch sticks open. What should you do?
options: Keep cutting, and push the lever closed by hand each time it sticks
Shut the gases off, tag the torch out of use and report it
Put a little oil on the lever so it moves freely
Tie the lever down with wire and carry on

questions.stem: What is the main reason for making a trial cut on scrap plate before cutting the real job?
options: To check the settings, speed and cut quality first
To use up gas left in the hoses from yesterday
To warm up the cutting table so the real job cuts faster
To give the slag tray something to collect

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What metal coating on gouging carbon electrodes helps them carry the current and last longer?
What is the name of the part fitted to a welding torch handle, in place of the welding nozzle, so the torch can be used to cut?

Which type of welding machine output, constant current or constant voltage, is normally used for air carbon arc gouging?

What is the name of a line marked a set distance from the cut line, so that the cut can be checked afterwards?

What is the name for the slot of metal removed by a flame or plasma cut?
On an air carbon arc gouging torch, what control turns the compressed air on and off?

essays.stem: Describe how to plan and set up for cutting a shaped part to a tight tolerance with oxy-fuel, from reading the drawing to making a trial cut.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the drawing for the shape, the sizes, the tolerance, the material and its thickness, and any bevels or holes. Check that the plate is the right grade and thickness and is flat and clean. Mark the shape out accurately from a datum with a scriber or soapstone, allowing for the kerf, and centre punch the centres of any holes and radii. Plan the order of cuts: cut holes and inside shapes first while the plate is still stiff, start each cut in the waste metal, and leave small tabs where long narrow parts might move. Choose the nozzle and the gas pressures from the maker's chart for the thickness. Set up guides, a template, a radius bar or a cutting trolley so that the torch follows the line steadily. Support the plate on the cutting table so the part will not drop or move when it comes free, and clear the area of anything that can burn. Then make a trial cut on a scrap of the same plate to check the flame, speed and cut quality, and adjust before cutting the job.
markingPoints: Drawing read for shape, sizes, tolerance and material; plate checked
Marked accurately from a datum, allowing for the kerf; centres punched
Cut order planned: holes and inner shapes first, starts in the waste, tabs where needed
Nozzle and pressures from the chart; guides, template or trolley set up; plate supported; area cleared
Trial cut on a scrap of the same plate to check settings and quality

essays.stem: Describe how to cut a 30° bevel with a root face on the edge of a 12 mm plate using a guide, and how you would check it.
essays.modelAnswer: Mark the bevel line on the top face of the plate. For a 30° bevel on 12 mm plate with a 2 mm root face, the bevel covers 10 mm of the thickness, so the line is about 5.8 mm in from the edge. Clamp a straight guide, or set the cutting trolley, so the nozzle runs along the line. Tilt the nozzle 30° from the vertical, towards the edge, and check the angle with a protractor. Set the nozzle and pressures from the chart, with a neutral preheat flame. Start at the end of the edge, preheat to bright red, open the cutting oxygen and travel at a steady speed, keeping the nozzle height and angle the same along the whole cut. The cut comes out through the edge about 2 mm above the bottom, leaving the root face; or the root face can be ground afterwards. Remove the slag. Check the bevel angle with a bevel protractor or weld gauge, measure the root face, check that the face is smooth with no notches, and grind out any small faults.
markingPoints: Bevel line marked correctly (about 5.8 mm in for 30° with a 2 mm root face on 12 mm plate), or set by the guide
Guide or trolley set; nozzle tilted 30° from vertical and checked
Chart settings, neutral preheat, start at bright red, steady speed with constant height and angle
Root face left by the cut or ground afterwards
Slag removed; angle checked with a gauge; root face measured; faults ground out

essays.stem: Explain how to pierce and cut a 100 mm diameter hole in 12 mm steel plate using a radius bar (circle-cutting guide).
essays.modelAnswer: Mark the centre of the hole and centre punch it deeply so that the radius bar's pivot point will not slip. Scribe or soapstone the 100 mm circle so that the cut can be checked. Fit the radius bar to the torch and set the distance from the pivot point to the cutting oxygen hole to the 50 mm radius, allowing for half the kerf so that the hole is not oversize, and check it with a rule. Choose the nozzle from the chart for 12 mm plate and set a neutral preheat flame. Because the hole is in the middle of the plate, pierce first in the waste metal inside the circle, away from the line. Preheat a spot to bright red, raise the nozzle a little and tilt it, then open the cutting oxygen slowly so that the slag blows away from the nozzle. When the jet is through, bring the nozzle upright and move out to the line, put the pivot point in the punch mark, and cut steadily round the circle. Watch that the slug does not drop onto your feet or the hoses.
markingPoints: Centre punched deeply; circle marked for checking
Radius bar set to the 50 mm radius, allowing for the kerf, and checked
Nozzle from the chart; neutral preheat flame
Pierced in the waste inside the circle: preheat, raise and tilt the nozzle, open the oxygen slowly
Moved out to the line, pivot in the punch mark, steady cut round; slug kept clear of feet and hoses

essays.stem: Describe the equipment and set-up for air carbon arc gouging, and the steps to gouge a groove in steel plate.
essays.modelAnswer: Air carbon arc gouging needs a welding power source that can give a high current, usually set to DC with the electrode positive (DCEP) for steel, a gouging torch with air jets, copper-coated carbon electrodes, and a clean, dry compressed-air supply at the pressure the maker gives. Check the cables, the air hose and the work clamp, and fix the clamp to clean metal near the job. Set up screens, clear anything that can burn, and place the work so that the molten metal blows away from people and equipment. Wear a welding helmet with a dark filter (about shade 12), ear protection, leather gloves and jacket, and boots. Set the current for the electrode size from the maker's chart. Fit the electrode with a short stick-out and with the air jets under it, between the electrode and the work. Turn the air on before striking the arc. Touch the electrode lightly on the work, then hold it at a push angle of about 35–45° and move forward steadily. Control the depth with the angle and the travel speed. Grind the groove before welding.
markingPoints: Equipment: high-current power source (usually DCEP), gouging torch, copper-coated carbon electrodes, clean dry compressed air
Checks and set-up: cables, hose, work clamp on clean metal; screens; fire precautions; metal stream directed safely
PPE: dark filter (about shade 12), ear protection, leather clothing
Current from the chart; short stick-out; air jets under the electrode; air on before striking
Steady push at a suitable angle; depth set by angle and speed; groove ground before welding

essays.stem: Explain the hazards of air carbon arc gouging, and how each one is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Noise: the arc and the air blast are very loud and can damage hearing, so wear ear plugs and ear muffs, and warn people nearby. Arc light: the arc gives strong ultraviolet and infrared light that can burn the eyes and skin, so wear a welding helmet with a dark filter, about shade 12 or as the chart says, and use screens to protect others. Molten metal and sparks: a large stream of molten metal is blown out, often several metres, which can burn people and start fires. Point it away from people, hoses, cylinders and anything that can burn, clear the area, keep an extinguisher ready, and keep a fire watch after the work. Wear leather gloves, a jacket and boots. Fumes: gouging gives off a lot of fume and smoke, especially on coated steel, so use extraction or good ventilation, and a respirator if needed. Electric shock: the machine runs at a high current, so check the cables, keep dry and fix the work clamp properly. Compressed air: never point the air jet at anyone. Hot stubs: put them in a metal container.
markingPoints: Noise — ear plugs and muffs
Arc light — dark filter (about shade 12) and screens
Molten metal and sparks — directed away from people and combustibles, area cleared, extinguisher, fire watch, leather PPE
Fumes — extraction or ventilation, respirator
Electric shock, compressed air and hot stubs controlled

essays.stem: Compare oxy-fuel gouging, air carbon arc gouging and plasma gouging. Say how each one works and when each is best used.
essays.modelAnswer: Oxy-fuel gouging uses a curved gouging nozzle on an oxy-fuel torch. The preheat flames heat the steel and a low-speed stream of oxygen burns it out, forming a groove. It needs no electricity, so it is useful on site and for carbon steel, but it is slower, puts a lot of heat into the job, and does not work on stainless steel or aluminium. Air carbon arc gouging uses an electric arc between a carbon electrode and the work to melt the metal, and a jet of compressed air blows it away. It is fast and works on most metals, including stainless steel and cast iron, and it is the usual way to remove faulty welds and to back-gouge heavy work. It is very noisy, makes a lot of fume and molten metal, and the groove must be ground before welding. Plasma gouging uses a plasma torch with a gouging tip held at a low angle. It is cleaner and quieter than air carbon arc gouging, gives good control and works on all metals that conduct electricity, so it suits lighter work and stainless steel, but the equipment costs more.
markingPoints: Oxy-fuel gouging: curved nozzle; preheat and low-speed oxygen burn out the groove; carbon steel and site work; slower, more heat
Air carbon arc gouging: carbon electrode arc melts the metal, compressed air blows it away
Air carbon arc: fast, most metals, removing faulty welds; noisy and fumy, groove ground after
Plasma gouging: plasma torch with a gouging tip at a low angle
Plasma: cleaner, quieter, good control, all conducting metals; dearer equipment

essays.stem: Describe how to remove a cracked or faulty weld by gouging, and prepare the groove for re-welding.
essays.modelAnswer: First find the full size of the fault. Clean the weld and look closely along it, using dye penetrant or another test if the Centre has one, to find both ends of the crack. Mark the area to be removed, a little beyond each end. Get permission and set up for gouging safely, with screens, fire precautions and the right PPE. Gouge along the fault in shallow passes, starting a little before one end and finishing a little past the other, so that none of the crack is left. Check the groove often, because a crack can go deeper than it looks. When the fault seems to be gone, grind the groove to remove the carbon-rich skin and any slag, and give it a smooth U shape with sloping ends so that it can be welded easily. Check the groove again, for example with dye penetrant, to prove that the crack has been fully removed. Preheat if the procedure asks for it, then reweld following the welding procedure, and inspect the repair.
markingPoints: Fault fully found (both ends of the crack, e.g. by dye penetrant) and marked a little beyond
Safe set-up: permission, screens, fire precautions, PPE
Gouged in shallow passes past each end, checking as it goes
Groove ground to remove the carbon-rich skin, shaped as a smooth U with sloping ends
Checked again to prove the fault is gone; preheat if required; rewelded to the procedure and inspected

essays.stem: Explain why plates and strips distort during thermal cutting, and describe ways to reduce it.
essays.modelAnswer: Distortion happens because the cut edge is heated and expands while the rest of the plate stays cool. When the hot edge cools, it shrinks and pulls, so long narrow strips bow, plates bend, and holes or shapes may move. Stresses already locked into the plate from rolling can also be released by the cut. The more heat that goes in, and the narrower the part, the worse the distortion. Ways to reduce it include: cutting both sides of a long strip at the same time with two torches, so both edges heat and shrink together; leaving small tabs (bridges) uncut until last, so the part is held in place; planning the cut order, such as cutting inner holes first and the outside last, and starting from the waste side; using the smallest nozzle that will do the job, at a steady and correct speed, so less heat goes in; clamping or weighting the plate so it cannot move; and choosing plasma for thin plate, because it is faster and puts in less heat. Parts that still bend can be straightened afterwards with heat or a press.
markingPoints: Cause: the cut edge heats and expands, then shrinks on cooling and pulls the part (locked-in stresses too)
Two torches cutting both sides of a strip at once
Tabs left until last, and a planned cut order (inner shapes first)
Less heat: smallest suitable nozzle, correct speed; plasma for thin plate
Clamping or weighting the plate; straightening afterwards if needed

essays.stem: Describe how to cut a steel pipe square, and with a bevel for welding, by hand, and how to check the cut.
essays.modelAnswer: Mark a square cut line round the pipe with a wraparound strip and soapstone or a scriber, and mark the waste side. Put the pipe on vee blocks or a stand at a comfortable height, chocked so it cannot roll, with the waste end overhanging so it can fall clear. Choose the nozzle from the chart for the wall thickness and set a neutral preheat flame. Start at the top, preheat to bright red and open the cutting oxygen. Keep the nozzle square to the pipe surface at every point, pointing at the centre of the pipe, and follow the line, moving your body or turning the pipe as you go. For a bevel, tilt the nozzle to the bevel angle the procedure gives, often about 30° to 37.5°, while still following the line, or use a pipe bevelling guide. Watch that the cut-off end does not drop onto your feet or the hoses. Remove the slag, check the cut with a square or wraparound and the bevel angle with a gauge, then grind the root face and clean the bevel before fitting up.
markingPoints: Square line marked with a wraparound; waste side marked
Pipe supported and chocked, with the waste end free to fall clear
Chart nozzle and neutral preheat; nozzle kept square to the surface, pointing at the centre
Bevel: nozzle tilted to the procedure angle (or a guide used) while following the line
Slag removed; squareness and bevel angle checked; root face ground and bevel cleaned

essays.stem: Describe what you inspect on a finished cut or gouge, the common faults you may find, and how each one is corrected.
essays.modelAnswer: Check the size and shape against the drawing with a rule, tape, square and templates, and the bevel angle and root face with a gauge, within the tolerance given. Look at the cut face: it should be smooth and square, with fine drag lines, a sharp top edge and little dross. Check a gouged groove for even depth and width and a smooth bottom. Common faults: a rounded, melted top edge, from too much preheat, a nozzle that is too close or travel that is too slow; correct the settings, and grind the edge if the part can still be used. Heavy dross stuck to the bottom, from travel that is too slow or low oxygen; chip and grind it off and adjust the speed. Notches or gouges in the face, where the torch stopped or wandered; grind them out smoothly, or weld and grind them if they are deep and the procedure allows. A bevel or face that is not square, from a tilted nozzle; adjust the guide and recut. A part that is out of tolerance must be reported, not hidden. Record the results.
markingPoints: Size, shape, bevel angle and root face checked against the drawing and tolerance with suitable tools
Cut face and gouge quality checked (square, smooth, fine drag lines, little dross, even groove)
Fault: rounded top edge, with cause and correction
Fault: heavy dross or notches, with cause and correction
Out-of-square or out-of-tolerance parts corrected or reported; results recorded

practical1.title: Cut a weld bevel, a hole and a template shape in 12 mm plate
practical1.brief: Each member of the group cuts three features in 12 mm mild steel plate with an oxy-acetylene cutting torch: (1) a 30° bevel along a 200 mm edge, using a guide or cutting trolley, then a 2 mm root face ground on it; (2) a 75 mm diameter hole, pierced in the waste and cut with a radius bar; and (3) a gusset shape cut round a sheet-steel template that the group makes and checks first. The group shares two cutting stations; members who are not cutting help to check the set-up, watch for fire and measure the parts. Each member measures their own bevel angle, root face, hole diameter and gusset sizes, and writes them on a results card. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Oxy-acetylene cutting outfits with flashback arrestors and check valves (two stations)
Cutting nozzles to suit 12 mm plate from the maker's chart, tip cleaners and a spark lighter
12 mm mild steel plate, about 300 mm × 250 mm, for each member
Straight-edge guide or cutting trolley, radius bar and G-clamps
Thin sheet steel for the gusset template
Bevel protractor or weld gauge, rule, tape, square, scriber, soapstone and centre punch
Angle grinder, chipping hammer, cutting table with slag tray, tongs and fire extinguisher
photos: Each plate marked out with the bevel line, hole centre and gusset outline
The guide or trolley set up with the nozzle tilted to 30°
The finished bevel being checked with a gauge, with the root face showing
Piercing in the waste of the hole, and the radius bar in use
The gusset cut round the template, beside the template
Every member's parts and results card laid out, with the area cleaned
checklist: Wore the correct PPE, including goggles with a suitable shade
Checked and leak-tested the outfit and set a neutral preheat flame
Bevel 30° within about 2.5°, smooth and even, with a 2 mm root face (within about 1 mm)
Pierced safely in the waste, with the nozzle raised and tilted
Hole 75 mm within about 1.5 mm, round and clean
Gusset matches the template within about 1.5 mm, with no deep notches
Measured and recorded their own results correctly
Shut down correctly and left the area safe and clean
safety: Cylinders chained upright and the outfit leak-tested; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Cut only over the cutting table with a slag tray; clear or cover anything that can burn for at least 10 m
Watch where the slug and cut-offs will fall; keep feet and hoses clear
Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding; check the disc and the guard
Treat all cut parts as hot: use tongs and mark them HOT

practical2.title: Air carbon arc gouging: gouge a groove and remove a fillet weld
practical2.brief: With the instructor present, the group sets up an air carbon arc gouging station: power source on DC electrode positive, gouging torch, compressed air, screens, and a safe direction for the molten metal. Each member then (1) gouges a straight groove about 150 mm long and about 5 mm deep in 12 mm mild steel plate, and (2) removes a 150 mm length of fillet weld from a scrap tee joint without gouging deeply into the plate. Each member grinds their groove clean and measures its depth and width. Members who are not gouging act as the fire watch and keep others clear. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the area is clean and the stubs are in a metal container.
materials: Welding power source suitable for gouging, set to DC electrode positive
Air carbon arc gouging torch and a clean, dry compressed-air supply
Copper-coated carbon electrodes, of the size the instructor gives
12 mm mild steel plate, about 200 mm × 150 mm, for each member
Scrap fillet-welded tee joints, one for each member
Angle grinder, rule and depth gauge
Welding screens, fire extinguisher and a metal container for stubs
photos: The gouging station set up, with screens and the metal stream pointed safely
A member in full PPE, including ear protection and a dark filter
Each member's groove just after gouging
The groove after grinding, with its depth being measured
The fillet weld removed from the tee joint
The stubs in a metal container and the area cleaned
checklist: Wore full PPE: helmet with a dark filter (about shade 12), ear protection, leather gloves, jacket and boots
Checked the cables, air hose and work clamp, and fixed the clamp to clean metal
Fitted the electrode with a short stick-out and the air jets under it, and turned the air on before striking
Kept a steady angle and speed, giving a straight groove of even depth (about 5 mm, within about 1.5 mm)
Removed the fillet weld without deep gouges in the plate
Ground the groove clean of the carbon-rich skin and measured it
Directed the molten metal safely and put hot stubs in the metal container
Shut down correctly (power off, air closed) and left the area safe
safety: Point the stream of molten metal away from people, hoses, cylinders and anything that can burn; use screens
Wear ear protection: the process is very loud
Never point the compressed-air jet at anyone
Keep a fire watch during the work and for a set time after it stops, as the Centre's rules say
Make sure there is good ventilation or extraction for the fumes; follow the maker's instructions
